headline: strong
texts: You read this obstruction module the way a good registrar reads a case: setting, level, strangulation, then the plan. No core objective came out as a gap. Keep the review cards on their schedule, because the exam traps here (old keys, look-alike signs, timings) fade fast without repetition.
Most-common-cause questions held: you read the age, site and setting before answering, and you can give the old exam key and the current answer together.
You sorted causes by their relation to the bowel wall, which lets you place a cause you have never memorised.
You derived the cardinal features from the level of the block rather than recalling a table, and you kept mechanical and adynamic obstruction apart.
You picked out strangulation from the change in pain and the systemic signs, which is the skill that decides who goes to theatre.
You told small from large bowel on film by the folds and the 3-6-9 numbers.
You separated the first test from the definitive one for obstruction and for paediatric intussusception.
Imaging signs were matched to disease and modality correctly.
You handled the management order: resuscitate, screen for strangulation, hernia and closed loop, then allow a timed trial.
You judged hernia risk by anatomy and kept the eponyms apart.
You used age to choose between enema and resection in intussusception.
You matched site to treatment for volvulus and obstructing cancer, and kept the caecum as the perforation site.
Drug and treatment of choice for gallstone ileus, Ogilvie's and paralytic ileus were secure.
Your confidence tracked your accuracy: Sure answers were right, and any Guessing answers mark what to review first. That is a useful revision signal, so trust it and start with the items you flagged.
You answered a diagnostic correctly and confidently and skipped a worked explanation. That is the right use of the fast lane. The traps still appear later, so stay alert for them.
No gaps and nothing shaky. Review the cards at 1, 3, 7, 21 and 60 days to hold this, and test yourself on the PYQ-versus-current-practice pairs, which are the likeliest to slip.
